name: The Pythagorean 'central fire' cosmology
plain_explanation: A group of Pythagoreans, attributed to Philolaus, proposed that the earth is not the center of the universe but one of ten heavenly bodies (including a hypothetical 'counter-earth') all orbiting a central fire, invisible to the Mediterranean world because the earth always turns the same face away from it -- a scheme that was largely wrong in its details but that made the crucial imaginative leap of removing the earth from the center of the cosmos.
precise_definition: The cosmological system attributed to Philolaus (late fifth century BC), in which the earth, sun, moon, five known planets, a hypothetical counter-earth, and a central fire ('the house of Zeus') together made up ten heavenly bodies (matching the mystically significant Pythagorean number ten), all orbiting the central fire, with the earth rotating so as to keep its inhabited face perpetually turned away from it, and the sun shining by light reflected from the central fire.
why_it_mattered: Russell calls it 'very important, since it involves the greater part of the imaginative effort required for conceiving the Copernican hypothesis': displacing the earth from the cosmic center, even fancifully and for mixed scientific and numerological reasons, was the psychologically difficult step, after which 'it was not so very difficult to be led by scientific arguments to a more accurate theory.'
historical_origin: Attributed to Philolaus, a Theban Pythagorean of the late fifth century BC.
examples: The counter-earth's postulated existence rested partly on a genuine observation (a lunar eclipse sometimes occurring while both sun and moon are above the horizon, actually caused by refraction, unknown to the Pythagoreans) and partly on numerology (needing exactly ten heavenly bodies).
objections: The central fire and counter-earth were themselves dropped by later Pythagoreans, soon after Plato's time, once observational astronomy advanced further.
competing_positions: The traditional geocentric picture it displaced, and the later, more scientifically grounded heliocentric hypothesis of Aristarchus that built on its central insight.
influence_on_later_thinkers: Prepared the conceptual ground for Heraclides's and, above all, Aristarchus's later heliocentric proposals.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: The central fire was given the religious names 'the house of Zeus' and 'the Mother of the gods,' reflecting its Pythagorean-mystical, not purely astronomical, motivation.
